rows.stem:
Consider the following standard electrode potential values :
\(\mathrm{Sn^{2+}_{(aq)}} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sn_{(s)}}\)   \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}} = -\ 0.14\) V
\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}_{(aq)}} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}_{(aq)}}\)   \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}} = +\ 0.77\) V
What is the cell reaction and potential for the spontaneous reaction that occurs ?
rows.solution:
The spontaneous reaction is \(2\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + \mathrm{Sn} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{Sn^{2+}}\), with \(E^{\circ} = +0{\cdot}91\) V.

The couple with the HIGHER reduction potential goes FORWARD as written, and the other is reversed. Iron(III) at \(+0{\cdot}77\) V therefore takes the electrons, and tin metal at \(-0{\cdot}14\) V gives them up.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}77 - (-0{\cdot}14) = +0{\cdot}91\ \mathrm{V}\)

Each option is wrong in its own way. The two reactions written with tin(II) being REDUCED run the wrong direction — one of them quotes a negative potential, correctly recognising that it is non-spontaneous, while the other pairs a reversed reaction with a positive value. The remaining option has the right reaction but ADDS the two potentials to get 1.68, instead of subtracting.

Note the factor of 2 in the equation, needed to balance the electrons: tin gives up two, and each iron(III) takes one. That factor never enters the potential, which is an INTENSIVE property.

rows.stem: The unit of molar conductivity is
rows.solution:
The unit of molar conductivity is \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

Derive it rather than remembering it. Molar conductivity is the conductivity divided by the concentration:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{\mathrm{C}}\)

Conductivity \(\kappa\) has units \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\), and concentration expressed per cubic centimetre has \(\mathrm{mol\ cm^{-3}}\):
\(\dfrac{\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}}{\mathrm{mol\ cm^{-3}}} = \mathrm{S\ cm^{2}\ mol^{-1}}\)

The \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) in the denominator becomes \(\mathrm{cm^{+3}}\) on top and combines with \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) to give \(\mathrm{cm^{2}}\).

The quantity also has a physical meaning that fixes the units: it is the conductance of a solution containing one MOLE of electrolyte, placed between electrodes one centimetre apart — so it is a conductance in siemens, multiplied by an AREA in \(\mathrm{cm^2}\), per mole. In SI the unit is \(\mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}}\), and \(1\ \mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}} = 10^4\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

rows.stem: Out of the following 1.0 M aqueous solutions, which one will show largest freezing point depression ?
rows.solution:
ALUMINIUM SULPHATE shows the largest depression in freezing point.

Depression of freezing point is COLLIGATIVE, depending on the number of PARTICLES rather than on what they are. All four solutions are 1.0 M, so the comparison reduces to the van't Hoff factor.

Count the ions each formula unit releases:
Glucose does not dissociate at all, \(i = 1\)
Sodium chloride gives \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), \(i = 2\)
Sodium sulphate gives two sodium ions and a sulphate, \(i = 3\)
Aluminium sulphate gives TWO \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) and THREE \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\), \(i = 5\)

Five is the largest, so that solution freezes lowest — about five times the depression glucose would give at the same molarity.

The number of ions is what counts, not the charge on them or the mass of the salt. A triply charged ion still counts as one particle.

rows.stem:
In the reaction
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\ \mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} + 3\mathrm{B} + 3\mathrm{C}\) the product A is
rows.solution:
The product A is PHENYL ISOCYANIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NC}\).

This is the CARBYLAMINE REACTION. A primary amine heated with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives an isocyanide, recognised at once by its exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

So B is potassium chloride and C is water, three of each, which matches the coefficients in the equation given.

The nitrogen stays attached to the ring and picks up the chloroform's CARBON — the attacking species being dichlorocarbene, generated when the alkali removes chloroform's hydrogen.

Note the difference from the CYANIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CN}\), where the ring carbon is bonded to the nitrile carbon. In the ISOCYANIDE the ring is bonded to the NITROGEN, which is why the reaction works only for a primary amine: the nitrogen must give up BOTH of its hydrogens.

rows.stem: \(\beta\)-pleated sheet structure in proteins refers to
rows.solution:
The \(\beta\)-pleated sheet is a SECONDARY structure.

The four levels of protein structure describe different things, and the \(\beta\)-sheet belongs firmly to the second.

PRIMARY is the SEQUENCE of amino acids, held by peptide bonds. SECONDARY is the local shape the chain adopts — the \(\alpha\)-helix and the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet — held by HYDROGEN BONDS between the backbone \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) and \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) groups. TERTIARY is the overall folding of the whole chain, held by disulphide bridges, electrostatic and van der Waals forces as well. QUATERNARY is the assembly of SEVERAL chains, as in haemoglobin's four.

In the \(\beta\)-sheet the chains are stretched nearly flat and lie side by side, with the hydrogen bonds running BETWEEN neighbouring stretches rather than within one coil — which is the difference from the \(\alpha\)-helix. Silk fibroin is the classic example.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The backbone of DNA and RNA molecules is a chain consisting of heterocyclic base, pentose sugar and phosphate group.
Reason (R) : Nucleotides and nucleosides mainly differ from each other in presence of phosphate group.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The Assertion is correct: a nucleic acid chain is built from units each containing a heterocyclic BASE, a pentose SUGAR and a PHOSPHATE group. Within that chain it is specifically the sugar and the phosphate that alternate to form the backbone, with the bases projecting from it — the phosphate linking the \(\mathrm{C_3}\) of one sugar to the \(\mathrm{C_5}\) of the next.

The Reason is also correct. A NUCLEOSIDE is base plus sugar; a NUCLEOTIDE is base plus sugar plus PHOSPHATE, and the phosphate is the whole of the difference.

But the two statements answer different questions. The Reason distinguishes two isolated units from each other; the Assertion describes what the polymer is made of. Knowing which of the two carries a phosphate does not explain the structure of the chain, although both facts concern the same molecules.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of reaction is applicable to elementary as well as complex reactions.
Reason (R) : For a complex reaction molecularity has no meaning.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The Assertion is correct. ORDER is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity, read off the measured rate law, so it can be determined for any reaction whose rate can be measured — elementary or complex alike. It may come out zero, fractional or even negative.

The Reason is also correct. MOLECULARITY counts the species colliding in a SINGLE elementary step, so it is defined only for such a step. A complex reaction is a sequence of steps, each possibly with its own molecularity, and the sequence as a whole has none to quote.

But the Reason is about MOLECULARITY and the Assertion about ORDER. That molecularity fails for complex reactions does not explain why order succeeds for them — it merely states the contrasting half of the same distinction. Both facts are worth knowing, and they stand side by side rather than one resting on the other.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The final product in Aldol condensation is always \(\alpha\), \(\beta\)-unsaturated carbonyl compound.
Reason (R) : \(\alpha\), \(\beta\)-unsaturated carbonyl compounds are stabilised due to conjugation.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

An aldol CONDENSATION runs in two stages. First the ADDITION: the enolate of one molecule attacks the carbonyl carbon of another, giving a \(\beta\)-hydroxy carbonyl compound, the aldol itself. Then the ELIMINATION of water, giving the \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

The Reason explains why the second stage happens. In the product the new \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) is CONJUGATED with the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\), so the \(\pi\) electrons are delocalised over all four atoms. That delocalisation lowers the energy of the product substantially, and it is what drives the dehydration.

An ordinary alcohol does not lose water so readily; the aldol does, often on gentle warming alone, because of the stability waiting on the other side.

The distinction worth holding onto is that the aldol ADDITION product can be isolated under mild conditions, but the CONDENSATION is defined as including the dehydration — so its final product is always the unsaturated compound.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5\ SO_4]}\ \mathrm{Cl}\) gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate solution.
Reason (R) : The complex dissociates to give \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) ions.
rows.context: For questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

The Assertion holds. In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) the square brackets enclose cobalt with five ammines and the sulphate; the CHLORIDE lies outside as the counter ion. Only what is outside ionises:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-}\)

That free chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride with silver nitrate.

The Reason is wrong about the SULPHATE. It does NOT come off — it is a LIGAND, bonded directly to the cobalt inside the coordination sphere, and a ligand is not released into solution. So the compound gives chloride ions but no free sulphate, and it yields NO precipitate with barium chloride.

That contrast is the whole point of the pair. Its ionisation isomer, \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\), behaves the other way round: it gives a precipitate with barium chloride and none with silver nitrate. Each fails the other's test, which is how the two are told apart.

rows.stem: Why haloarenes are not reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ? Give two reasons.
rows.solution:
Haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution for several reasons; any two of the following.

RESONANCE. The halogen's lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the carbon-halogen bond PARTIAL DOUBLE BOND CHARACTER. That makes the bond shorter and stronger than in an alkyl halide, and far harder to break — and breaking it is what the substitution requires.

HYBRIDISATION. The carbon bearing the halogen is \(sp^2\) in a haloarene but \(sp^3\) in a haloalkane. An \(sp^2\) orbital has more s character, so it is smaller and holds its electrons more tightly, giving a shorter and stronger bond again.

REPULSION BY THE \(\pi\) CLOUD. The benzene ring is electron rich on both faces, so an approaching nucleophile — itself electron rich — is REPELLED rather than attracted, and the backside approach that an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction needs is blocked by the ring.

INSTABILITY OF THE PHENYL CATION. An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) route is closed too, because the cation that would have to form is not stabilised by resonance, its empty orbital lying in the plane of the ring rather than perpendicular to it.

rows.stem: Give the reaction of heating glucose with hydroxylamine. Presence of which group is confirmed by this reaction ?
rows.solution:
Hydroxylamine CONDENSES with the carbonyl group of glucose, losing water:
\(\mathrm{CH_2OH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2NOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_2OH{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH{=}NOH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is GLUCOSE OXIME.

The reaction confirms the presence of a CARBONYL group. Condensing with an ammonia derivative in this way is characteristic of an aldehyde or ketone, and of no other group in the molecule — the several hydroxyls do not react with hydroxylamine at all.

To narrow the carbonyl down to an ALDEHYDE rather than a ketone, a further test is needed, and glucose supplies it by reducing Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.

The same reaction gave a decisive piece of negative evidence: glucose PENTA-ACETATE, in which all five hydroxyls are esterified, does NOT form an oxime. With the anomeric hydroxyl locked up the ring can no longer open, no aldehyde is ever present, and that is one of the observations that established the cyclic structure.

rows.stem:
(a) On the basis of crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^4}\) with a strong field ligand for which \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\).
(b) A solution of \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) is green but a solution of \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is colourless. Explain.
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(a) The configuration is \(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^0\).

An octahedral field splits the d orbitals into a lower set of three and an upper set of two, separated by \(\Delta_0\). Each electron entering chooses between promotion to the upper set, costing \(\Delta_0\), and pairing in the lower set, costing the pairing energy \(\mathrm{P}\).

The question specifies \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) — a STRONG FIELD — so PAIRING is the cheaper option. The first three electrons occupy the three lower orbitals singly, and the fourth PAIRS UP in the lower set rather than going upstairs.

The result is a LOW SPIN complex with TWO unpaired electrons, \(\mu = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

A WEAK field would have given \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\) instead — four unpaired electrons and \(\mu = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M. The same \(d^4\) ion gives different magnetic behaviour depending only on the ligand, and the fourth electron is where the two cases part company.

(b) Because one ion has a PARTLY FILLED d subshell and the other a COMPLETELY FILLED one.

Colour in these compounds arises from a D-D TRANSITION: an electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper, and what remains of the white light is the colour seen. The jump needs an ELECTRON below and a VACANCY above.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\) nickel is \(+2\), that is \(3d^8\). Water is a weak field ligand, so the electrons stay spread out with vacancies in the upper set, the splitting is small, and the absorption falls in the visible — the solution is GREEN.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the ZERO state, \(3d^8 4s^2\), and carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the d set to give \(3d^{10}\). With every d orbital FULL there is no vacancy anywhere, no d-d transition is possible, and the compound is COLOURLESS.

rows.stem: Why does conductivity increase though the conductivity decrease with dilution ?
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
[The stem as printed uses the word "conductivity" for both quantities; the contrast it asks about is between MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY, which increases on dilution, and CONDUCTIVITY, which decreases.]

The two move in opposite directions because they are measured against DIFFERENT THINGS.

CONDUCTIVITY \(\kappa\) is the conductance of a FIXED VOLUME of solution — the block held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. What carries the current is the ions inside that block, so \(\kappa\) depends on the number of ions PER UNIT VOLUME. Diluting spreads the same ions through more solution, so that fixed block holds fewer of them and conducts less.

MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY \(\Lambda_m\) is the conductance furnished by a FIXED AMOUNT of electrolyte — one mole of it, however much solvent that mole is spread through:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{\mathrm{C}}\)

The number of ions from that mole does not fall on dilution. For a strong electrolyte it stays the same and the ions merely move further apart, interfering with one another's migration less, so each carries current more freely. For a weak electrolyte more of the mole actually IONISES.

Rahul's table shows both effects at once: as the concentration falls from 1.00 M to 0.01 M, \(\kappa\) drops from \(111{\cdot}3 \times 10^{-3}\) to \(1{\cdot}41 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\) while \(\Lambda_m\) rises from 111.3 to 141.0.

rows.stem: Amit a classmate of Rahul repeated the same experiment with \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) solution instead of KCl solution. Give one point that would be similar and one that would be different in his observations as compared to Rahul.
rows.context:
Rahul set-up an experiment to find resistance of aqueous KCl solution for different concentrations at 298 K using a conductivity cell connected to a Wheatstone bridge. He fed the Wheatstone bridge with a.c. power in the audio frequency range 550 to 5000 cycles per second. Once the resistance was calculated from null point he also calculated the conductivity K and molar conductivity \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and recorded his readings in tabular form.

| S.No. | Conc.(M) | k S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) | \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. | 1.00 | \(111.3 \times 10^{-3}\) | 111.3 |
| 2. | 0.10 | \(12.9 \times 10^{-3}\) | 129.0 |
| 3. | 0.01 | \(1.41 \times 10^{-3}\) | 141.0 |
rows.solution:
SIMILARITY: in both cases the MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY INCREASES on dilution, while the CONDUCTIVITY itself DECREASES.

DIFFERENCE: the SHAPE of that increase, and what can be done with it.

For potassium chloride, a STRONG electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) rises only GRADUALLY — the salt is fully dissociated at every dilution, and the small rise merely reflects the ions interfering with one another less as they move apart. A plot against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is very nearly a straight line, so it can be extrapolated to zero concentration to give \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly.

For acetic acid, a WEAK electrolyte, \(\Lambda_m\) rises STEEPLY, and steepest of all near infinite dilution. The cause is different in kind: the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself is increasing, so one mole of acid furnishes more and more ions. The curve never straightens and never meets the axis, so \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) cannot be obtained by extrapolation at all and must be calculated from KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW instead.

Amit's absolute readings would also be much LOWER than Rahul's at every concentration, acetic acid being only slightly ionised.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) Write the number of unpaired electrons in \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\).
(Atomic number of Cr = 24)
(b) Complete the reaction mentioning all the products formed :
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2S} + 8\mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow\)
(c) Account for the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) towards oxidation to +3 state.
(ii) Copper has exceptionally positive \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) value.
(iii) \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) with electronic configuration [Xe] \(4\mathrm{f^7}6\mathrm{s^2}\) is a strong reducing agent.
rows.solution:
(a) THREE unpaired electrons.

Chromium is atomic number 24, so the atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1\). Removing three electrons — the single \(4s\) and two \(3d\) — leaves \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) as \(3d^3\).

Three electrons in five orbitals occupy three of them SINGLY by Hund's rule, so all three are unpaired and \(\mu = \sqrt{3 \times 5} = 3{\cdot}87\) B.M.

In an octahedral field those three fill the \(t_{2g}\) set exactly, a half-filled lower set that is unusually stable — which is why \(+3\) is the characteristic state of chromium.

(b) Dichromate oxidises hydrogen sulphide to SULPHUR, chromium falling from \(+6\) to \(+3\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2S} + 8\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{S} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Six electrons change hands: two chromium atoms take three each, and three sulphides give up two each, rising from \(-2\) to 0. The orange solution turns green and sulphur separates as a milky precipitate.

(c)(i) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ALREADY HAS the stable half-filled configuration, while \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) reaches it by being oxidised.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\) — exactly half filled, every orbital singly occupied with parallel spins, an arrangement of unusual stability. Oxidising it to \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) would DESTROY that arrangement, giving \(3d^4\), so manganese(II) resists oxidation.

\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\) — one electron beyond the stable set. Losing that electron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which IS \(3d^5\), so iron(II) is oxidised readily. A solution of an iron(II) salt turns yellow-brown in air for exactly this reason.

(ii) Because copper has a HIGH enthalpy of atomisation and a LOW hydration enthalpy.

Converting solid copper into hydrated copper(II) ions takes three steps, and the energy recovered in the last must pay for the first two. Pulling an atom out of the metal costs a great deal, removing two electrons costs more, and copper's hydration enthalpy is NOT large enough to cover both.

The books therefore do not balance, the process is unfavourable, and \(E^{\circ}\) comes out positive at \(+0{\cdot}34\) V — the only such value in the 3d series. This is why copper does not dissolve in hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid: it cannot displace hydrogen.

(iii) Because \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) readily changes to the \(+3\) state, which is the characteristic state of the lanthanoids.

Giving up an electron is what a reducing agent does, and europium(II) does it easily because europium(III) is the state the whole series prefers — held there by the lanthanoids' similar sizes and the energies of their \(4f\) orbitals. Europium(II) solutions therefore reduce water slowly and are oxidised by air.

[The stem gives europium(II) the configuration \([\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 6s^2\), which is the NEUTRAL ATOM. The ion \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) has lost those two \(6s\) electrons and is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7\). The marking scheme records the discrepancy and directs full marks for any attempt.]
